title: Improving Pop-Up Debates: Tracking the Argument
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart diagnoses recurring problems in his classroom pop-up debates: students disengage after speaking, repeat one another, and leave good arguments unaddressed. His single solution is mandatory tracking of the argument, a visual flowing method borrowed from Les Lynn that records each contribution on the board or document camera. Arguments are circled, counter-arguments and refutations are boxed and linked by arrows, and only new additive argumentation is recorded. He explains how tracking and occasionally calling arguments turns students from passive recipients into active evaluators. He ends by framing the work as improvement rather than perfection.
points: Poor listening, repetition and unaddressed arguments in discussion share one fix: mandatory visual tracking of the argument.
The tracking rules (circle arguments, box and arrow counter-arguments and refutations, record only additive claims) make the structure of a debate visible.
Asking speakers to restate or clarify while tracking signals responsibility for clarity and engages listeners.
Calling an argument won or drawn keeps the debate moving and models evaluation.
quotes: Problems like these have a single, simple solution: mandatory tracking of the argument. When our students (and us at first on the board or the doc cam) write down each student's contribution to a pop-up debate using a simple set of rules, we increase the quality of their listening and the quality of their resulting argumentation.

Each counter-argument is boxed and linked to the argument it responds to with an arrow. - Each refutation (an attempt at defeating a counter-argument) is also boxed and linked with an arrow to the counter-argument it responds to.
Only new, “additive” argumentation is tracked. If a student pops up and contributes something that repeats a prior argument or goes on an unproductive tangent, their arguments are not recorded.

As I'm doing this on the document camera during the debate, I'm frequently asking arguers to restate or clarify. This signals to arguers that they have a responsibility to be clear, and this tends to perk the ears of the listeners who are tracking the argument. They shift from passive recipients of pop-up debate speeches into active evaluators.

The “pop-up” format exists as a “simple to a fault” structure for facilitating and managing whole-class discussions, conversations, arguments, or even toasts. When we're putting together pop-up debates, our mentality has to be that of the improvementist versus the perfectionist. I hope that Les Lynn's visual tracking method can be a useful way for you and your students to improve.
